items.summary: Magma moving beneath a volcano can make the ground rise, sink or shift sideways. Measuring these changes gives scientists clues about where magma is stored and how it travels. items.title: It's hard to predict who will be suicidal: It's easier to ensure people can't shoot themselves
items.summary: Dr. Paul Nestadt is about as steeped in suicide prevention as a person can be.

items.title: Starch-based sensor changes color to indicate moisture in food packaging
items.summary: Brazilian researchers have developed a biodegradable, starch-based sensor that changes color when moisture enters food packaging. items.title: Gene editing produces soybean with more than 90% oleic acid
items.summary: Sejong University researchers have developed a high-quality soybean with improved oxidative stability, reduced saturated fat and increased seed fatty acid content. items.title: NASA Modernizes Commercial Airline Systems
items.summary: NASA’s researchers know that when you settle into your seat on a commercial flight, you expect a smooth takeoff, views over the clouds, a steady descent, and hopefully an early arrival at your destination. items.title: Bee-made propolis boosts an antifungal drug against yeast pathogens in lab tests
items.summary: Propolis may not only inhibit the growth of certain fungi but also affect the activity of drugs used to treat fungal infections. Researchers have investigated how an ethanolic extract of Polish propolis interacts with various antifungal agents.

items.title: Banking patterns could help identify people experiencing financial abuse, UK study finds
items.summary: Telltale signs of financial abuse, such as depleted savings, increasing debts and declining credit scores, can be identified in bank records, according to an analysis of U.K. banking data published in Nature. items.title: Central surface density of dark matter agrees with the prediction of a new theory of gravity
items.summary: A researcher from Sejong University has used a new theory of gravity proposed by Erik Verlinde to predict the observed central surface density of dark matter. The study was published in Physics of the Dark Universe on Sept. 20.

items.title: Aiming at number 9: CASPAR targets fluorine in new science run
items.summary: The Compact Accelerator System for Performing Astrophysical Research (CASPAR) recreates conditions inside stars to study how elements are made. The experiment recently restarted with a new target—the ninth element on the periodic table, fluorine.

items.title: The Antarctic's only two flowering plants reveal opposing strategies for surviving long-term warming
items.summary: A team of Chilean and Spanish researchers has published the results of one of the longest-running in-situ warming experiments in maritime Antarctica in the journal Physiologia Plantarum. items.summary: Scientists have shown that the two exponents (inelastic scattering exponent and dephasing exponent) commonly used to describe electron scattering in graphene do not necessarily follow the same behavior. items.title: How ChatGPT served up false information before the 2024 election
items.summary: On Oct. 25, 2024, 10 days before the election that would return Republican Donald Trump to the White House and more than three months after Kamala Harris ascended to the top of the Democratic ticket, ChatGPT was still telling users that Joe Biden was running for a second term as president.

items.title: Evolved enzymes build tuberculosis antibiotic ingredient in the desired form, potentially reducing waste
items.summary: Tuberculosis, or TB, is a contagious bacterial infection that primarily affects the lungs. items.title: New AI methodology powers the latest million dollar list
items.summary: New research from Indiana University Lilly Family School of Philanthropy examines charitable gifts of $1 million or more from 2021 to 2023. The Million-Dollar-Plus Giving in the United States, 2021–2023 report offers insights into how these donors responded to a rapidly changing environment.

items.title: Ancient genome function persists despite frequent mutations, centromere study shows
items.summary: Every time a cell divides, its chromosomes must be distributed correctly between the two daughter cells. Central to this process is the centromere, a specialized region of the chromosome. The centromere serves as the attachment site for the cellular machinery that pulls the chromosomes apart.

items.title: Cooling investments in apparel factories can pay for themselves, study shows
items.summary: Investing in cooling for Bangladesh's apparel factories can be commercially viable, with an average payback period of one to four years, according to new research from Cornell University's Global Labor Institute (GLI).

items.title: Scientists build world's most accurate atomic clock
items.summary: Take a second and turn it into trillions of moments. Measure each one. That's how precisely an atomic clock at Singapore's Centre for Quantum Technologies (CQT) keeps time—and with record-setting accuracy, according to results published in Nature on Sept. 23.

items.title: NASA Selects Far-Infrared Telescope as First in New Mission Class
items.summary: NASA announced Wednesday a mission to explore the history and evolution of the universe, PRIMA (PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics), is advancing to the next phase of development. items.title: Political shifts may shape how quickly Germany adopts electric cars and solar power
items.summary: A new study conducted by the Climate Action Research Lab (CARL) at the University of Freiburg finds that electric cars and photovoltaic systems are less widespread on average in municipalities with strong support for Alternative for Germany (AfD). items.title: Prefer intricate shapes? You may also favor complex melodies
items.summary: A shape can be considered complex because it has many sides. A complex melody may feature varied pitches and rhythms. Does the mind treat these as separate features, or can it recognize something common beneath their differences?

items.title: Unevenness of global warming: Regional warming speedups emerge in waves
items.summary: New research from the University of California, Santa Cruz, in collaboration with other institutions, highlights the fragmented and staggered timing of warming increases across the planet, providing a nuanced perspective on the debate over global-warming acceleration.

items.title: Palette versus palate: Wine drinkers embrace a spectrum of wine colors
items.summary: When a glass of red wine arrives at the table, most drinkers make a snap judgment before taking a sip. Is the color deep enough? Does the hue suggest quality or raise a red flag?
